We live in an era of financial decline. Such an era of decline can be exciting. Compare our era, the early 10's, to the early 80's. The early 80's seem as if despite decline, people were having fun and it was a reasonably exciting time to be around. In practice, ours sadly isn't. I'm obviously not exactly sure why, but I have noticed some factors that I think are crucially important. I think one factor that's different today from the 80's is that there is far more centralized control today than there was in the early 80's. One reason for this is that there is now more advanced technology that simply enables centralized control, another reason is that an increasing lack of cultural cohesion means that our society is less willing to accept risks and social experiments.

Let's look at some of these technological factors. Here is an example: Back in the 80's, you might have bluffed your way into a job where you don't belong. In the 2010's, that looks very unlikely, because there exists such a thing as the Internet. If you don't have a linkedin profile that lists what you spent the last five years of your life doing, employers will assume the worst about you. If you did anything scandalous, chances are your name can be found on the internet as well.

The effect it has is that people become more conservative and risk-averse, especially intelligent people. You need to have your life on track, because if you don't, everyone can see you're not the ideal employee. Back in earlier days, us non-ideal employees were much harder to distinguish from ideal employees, thus we had a reasonable chance of living quite a pleasant life. Today however, it's a lot easier for employers to recognize us. "Why doesn't his profile here say anything about these extracurricular activities he supposedly engaged in back in college?" In fact, even not having a Facebook account can be enough for employers to discriminate against you.

There are other factors too that make our era relatively boring. Young people don't really have the time or the financial ability anymore to maintain their own subculture. Young people are forced to go to college, which has become the new high school diploma. In my country at least, college was a time that the upper class could fill their whole twenties with. Today, costs have increased and this is no longer viable. Young people in fact increasingly face college debts, which are much more serious than other types of debt, as you generally can't default on them. Note also that debts today are much harder to escape from in general, as those with debts can be easily found on the Internet.

The Dutch government outlawed squatting a few years ago. This is the type of social atmosphere the disenfranchised are attracted to, where new cultural movements emerge. It was very important in the 80's. In fact, there's a growing industry of vacant property management corporations, that look for particular personality types they can dump into unused buildings on behalf of their owners. They establish strict rules there, so you're not allowed to hold parties and can be kicked out any moment, even though many of the best clubs in Amsterdam today grew out of buildings that were once taken over by squatters.

Also worth noting is that, contrary to what you might think, you had more flexibility back in earlier days. As an example, it used to be quite normal for an optician to have no degree beyond a high school degree. After all, the worst that could reasonably happen would be that someone ends up with poor glasses. Now, there's an abundance of labor, so what happens is that companies that sell glasses have ads on TV showing babyboomer actors who feign outrage over the fact that an optician didn't go to school to become an optician. Then, the company proudly proclaims that "all of our opticians are certified"! The consequence of this is that optician is a job you can no longer roll into or out of, rather it's something you'll probably find yourself doing throughout your life.

This might seem like a rare example, but I can look at my dad and recognize that the diverse variety of jobs he rolled into would be impossible for people my age. He was drafted into the army, where he got a driver's license. Back in those days, you could qualify for just about any driving license, if you passed one of them. As a result, despite never having seen the inside of a truck, my dad became licensed to drive a truck. He didn't know back then that this license would come in quite useful later in life. He was laid off at his job at the government in the 90's, and eventually in the 2000's, after a number of temporary odd jobs, worked for a while as a truck driver. For me, or anyone else my age for that matter, this would be impossible, without first becoming licensed to operate a truck.

Now, what else makes our era so boring? Believe it or not, a surprising degree of social isolation. What we're doing here, typing on a screen, has largely replaced actual interaction. Part of the reason is simply the fact that this interaction is comparatively inexpensive. If you talk to friends on a screen, you save money, if you meet them in the local bar or shopping mall, you're spending money. The mall itself is a dying aspect of modern life, as is the bookstore and perhaps even the supermarket, thanks to the Internet. It needs to be noted that the supermarket of course was a deterioration compared to what preceded the supermarket, a variety of small family-owned businesses that specialized in cheese, herbs, meat, vegetables, liquor and God knows what more. Still, at least it is something reminiscent of a community center.

Of course you might say that nightlife is where we are supposed to interact, rather than the bookstore, the mall, or the supermarket, but nightlife itself is dying out. Compared to ten years ago, this country has about half as many discotheques. The parties I used to go to years ago are coming to an end, due to a lack of people attending and government policies increasing the price. It's probably going to get even worse the coming years, as a raise of the VAT will increase the price of public transport by fifteen percent in one go.

Altogether, I'm bored with our era. Without centralized control that seeks to preserve order, decline could be an exciting period. Sadly, it's not. The only advantage I have seen from the decline so far is that animal populations seem to recover. Wild animals of course, are one of the few factors not under the yoke of centralized control. With less people driving around in cars, less hedgehogs are turned into pulp. Thus, I manage to see hedgehogs around me. Hopefully, this trend can continue.
The tragedy of growing up in the dull era
I don't think I could express this idea any better. Now, I will say that making the decline boring is simply sadistic.

Per NWS in Melbourne, FL: Debris from the ‪#‎SpaceX‬ ‪#‎Falcon9‬ rocket failure was visible on our Doppler radar this morning. The rocket failure occurred at approximately 150,000 feet, so it took several minutes for the debris to become visible.

Correlation coefficient (CC) is one of the many tools we can use to see precipitation and non-precipitation targets, and it helped us spot the debris this morning. Correlation coefficient data tell us how similarly shaped things are in the atmosphere. For instance, rain often has HIGH correlation (maroon colors), while birds, bugs, and debris have LOW correlation values (blue colors).

What I mean by that is, what is a game that you have been playing this past week, and should we play it? Why?

Personally I bought and just finished Burial at Sea episode 2 and OH MY GOD BEST STORY EVER TOLD. The BioShock franchise is something I love and would be my favorite franchise if Half-Life wasn't a thing. If you have played BioShock 1 and BioShock: Infinite before, Burial at Sea ep 1 and 2 is something I wholeheartedly recommend, as it connects both stories in a very nice touch. If you have played only one of those, then don't, you'll be spoiling the whole story to yourself.

Standpoint: one I bought and finished before BaS. Cool indie first-person puzzle-platform, kinda niche, but challenging. Story is kind off "insipid" and I can't really relate to it but meh, cool game. I wouldn't totally recommend it... but check if it's your thing

Kung Fury: Street Rage: it's great, it plays like One Finger Death Punch, but feels lighter. Total approval on my point, and watch the movie too, it kicks ass.

Borealis: another indie I bought during the Steam sale. It says "bullet hell" in the popular user-defined tags, but it doesn't feel like Touhou or something like that. It is relaxing and chill to play, but not for everyone.

Frederic: Resurrection of Music: Guitar Hero for piano players. I don't know how to play an instrument, heck, I only learned how to play the flute in school when I was 12, but it's an ok game. It uses the keyboard and it's re-bindable, so that's good.

Love: although it can be beaten in less than 20 minutes and it's not difficult, the art style and the music are delightful. In terms of re-playability, I'm coming back to it for the achievements, but I've clocked more than 4 into it, it must be because of something. The speedrun and the #yolo modes also give quite of fun, frustation, and wanting to be the best.

Castle Crasher: I've heard only good things about this game, so it's time that I buy it... almost 3 years after it releases. Sadly, I have yet to play it because my timing with my friends sucks.

Two free, non-Steam games I play daily and recommend:

Town of Salem: it's a "burn the witch" kind of game. 15 people are given different roles, they have to accomplish their objective. Sometimes you have to kill everyone, sometimes you have to find the murderers. It's even more fun to play with friends.

Smite: like DotA/LoL but in 3rd person. For people like me that can't play top-down games (DotA, LoL, Heroes of the Storm, Diablo, Path of Exile, etc.) this one is a miracle from heaven. And I can't speak for other games' community, but I've heard it has a better community... still kinda flamy tho.
